Pain disrupts sleep, and there's noted difficulty with activities of daily living like brushing hair and dressing. No history of shoulder trauma, neck pain, arm/hand weakness, numbness, or paresthesias. The patient has type 2 diabetes mellitus, treated with metformin and glipizide.

Difficulty with brushing hair and dressing

patient_actor_hidden.Review_of_Systems: Denies neck pain, arm/hand weakness, numbness, or paresthesias.

objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with chronic left shoulder pain without a history of trauma.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, what brings you in today? Patient: I’ve had left shoulder pain for about two months that’s been slowly getting worse, especially when I move it to the extremes or use it, and it’s started to disrupt my sleep. It’s made daily tasks like brushing my hair and dressing difficult.
Doctor: Did the shoulder pain begin after any specific injury, fall, or new activity?
Patient: No, it didn’t start after any injury or fall, and I can’t think of any new activity that triggered it. It just seemed to build up gradually over the last two months.
Doctor: Can you describe the quality of the pain—does it feel sharp, dull, aching, burning, or something else?
Patient: It feels mostly aching and sore, but it also gets quite sharp when I move my left shoulder to the very far or extreme positions.
Doctor: Where exactly is the pain located—does it feel more on the front of the shoulder, the top, the back, or deep around the joint?
Patient: The pain feels deep around the left shoulder joint, more toward the top and outer side than the front or back.

Doctor: When you try to lift your arm or reach behind your back, do you notice any limitation in movement, and is the limitation different when someone else moves your arm for you (passive range of motion)?

Patient: Yes—lifting my arm and reaching behind my back are limited, and it’s very painful to push it to the farthest positions. When you move my arm for me, it still seems restricted and sore, though it feels a bit less painful than when I try to do it myself.
Doctor: Do you notice the pain worsening at night, especially when you lie on the affected side or try to sleep flat?
Patient: Yes, it definitely gets worse at night, especially if I try to lie on my left side, and it’s hard to get comfortable or sleep through it.
Doctor: Does the pain get worse when you lift your arm overhead or reach behind your head?

Patient: Yes—raising my arm overhead and reaching behind my head makes it much worse, and reaching behind my back is especially limited and painful. It hurts most at the extreme positions, no matter what angle I try to move it to.
Doctor: Do you notice a general stiffness or loss of motion in the shoulder even when you’re not in pain, such that it feels “tight” or “frozen” throughout the range

Patient: Yes, I feel stiff and “tight” in the left shoulder overall, and my range of motion feels noticeably reduced even beyond just when it hurts—especially with reaching behind my back or overhead. It feels like it doesn’t move as far as it used to, regardless of how gently I try.
Doctor: When you try to rotate your arm outward (external rotation) with your elbow bent at your side, is that movement limited or painful?
Patient: Yes, turning my arm outward is both limited and painful, especially when I try to get to the farthest range. It feels restricted and hurts most at the extremes.
Doctor: Do you notice any weakness when you try to lift objects with your left arm, especially when raising your arm to the side (abduction) or rotating it outward?

Patient: I don’t really notice weakness like my arm “can’t” do it, but using it—especially lifting or raising it out to the side or turning it outward—causes sharp pain and it limits what I’m able to do. I mostly feel restricted and sore rather than truly weak.
Doctor: Do you have any medical conditions such as diabetes, thyroid problems, or a history of previous shoulder issues or surgeries?
Patient: Yes, I have type 2 diabetes and take metformin and glipizide. I haven’t had any prior shoulder injuries, and I’ve never had shoulder surgery.
Doctor: Have you noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth over the left shoulder, or any fever or chills accompanying the pain?
Patient: I haven’t noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth over my left shoulder, and I don’t have fever or chills.
[DDX] Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), Rotator cuff tendinopathy/partial tear, Glenohumeral osteoarthritis, Subacromial bursitis, Cervical radiculopathy (C5‑C6)
